articles.title: Johnnette unveils JF-3 VTOL drone for ISTAR and artillery support
articles.text:
Noida-based Johnnette Technologies has unveiled the JF-3 VTOL, a fixed-wing unmanned aircraft designed for intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition and reconnaissance (ISTAR). Its vertical take-off and landing capability is intended to let it operate from locations without a runway, while its fixed-wing layout is designed for longer flights than a conventional multirotor.
The system has an endurance of 150 minutes, a range of 50km and mission payload capacity of 2kg. It weighs 17kg and has a maximum speed of 110km/h. However, from the product page, the weight is shown as 18kg with an endurance time of 2h 15m.
The system features an EO/IR payload with 4K video, 30x zoom lens, radiometric infrared and a laser range finder which can detect objects up to 2400m away. The VTOL system can be used for Direction of Own Artillery Fire (DOOAF), as the high vantage point allows crews to get an overview of the terrain. However there are no details regarding assessment of this capability within the announcement.
The JF-3 is equipped with protection against jamming and spoofing. It has navigation functionality that does not rely on GNSS, and frequency hopping data links to allow operation in hostile environments. It can be operated using the ground control station developed by Johnnette in order to plan missions and monitor in real time.
90% of the aircraft is locally made. How this value was determined is not specified, and no further information on what components were made in India is given.
This launch makes available a new tactical fixed-wing VTOL aircraft in India. As no specific customer was mentioned, or any decisions made to place an order for, or induct this aircraft, it should be considered that this aircraft is now available for potential military applications. It has not yet been decided by the armed forces that this will be the aircraft used.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: SpaceFields Successfully Hot-Fires 120mm and 165mm RATO Boosters at IISc Facility
articles.text:
Bengaluru-based deep-tech aerospace startup SpaceFields successfully tested and hot-fired various Rocket-Assisted Take-Off (RATO) boosters at its propulsion testing facility at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru.
RATO boosters are auxiliary rocket propulsion units to provide additional thrust during the initial take-off of an aircraft or unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV).
Company said ” we successfully hot-fired 120mm & 165mm Rocket-Assisted Take-Off (RATO) Boosters at Indian Institute of Science (IISc) facility.
Custom-engineered for various thrust profiles, designed for integration across diverse UAV platforms and tailored to meet mission-specific operational needs. ”
In September 2024, the company successfully conducted a hot-fire test of its aerospike rocket engine at its IISc Challakere facility.
Another successful hot-firing campaign was reported in January 2025, demonstrating a peak thrust of 13.42 kN.
In February 2024, the company raised approximately Rs 6.5 crore in its first institutional funding round.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: Project Vishnu: India’s First Powered Hypersonic Cruise Missile Moves Towards First Phase
articles.text:
DRDO in the last six years has moved from a sustained scramjet engine trial from 20 seconds to 1200 seconds, but the final approvals for the development are yet to come, but the things are moving towards final approvals as per sources close to IDRW, and the program will see the first development of a powered hypersonic cruise program taking off first, which will have a range of 1500 plus and will be able to hit Mach-8 from the start and will have the ability to dodge air defence systems.
IDRW has estimated that project funds could be over 5000 crores, and with the scramjet propulsion being validated in ground trials, more ground runs are being planned, and once the test results and data collected are completed and improvements and refinements are carried out, the programme could see the development of a missile airframe that can sustain the temperature at which the missile will operate and also the development of a seeker that can operate in such conditions.
Most of the materials that will be used have been identified and tested on a small scale, and more trials could require more funding, but the programme won’t suffer any research-related delays, as most of the progress that will go into the missile is more or less has been identified or developed in the laboratories. What needs to be done now is to put them together and validate the airframe with the scramjet engine before flight trials can commence.
In April 2026 DRDO began fabricating jigs and fixtures to mate the H1 booster with the scramjet alignment of centre lines, structural integrity under launch loads, and repeatable assembly tolerances. Officials described this as a necessary step before structural assembly and integrated testing of the vehicle can begin.
DRDO expects trials to be completed by 2032-33 once the programme is approved, and trials of flightworthy airframes could start by 2030 onwards. That could see the first development of a ground-launched variant that can travel at Mach 7-8 speeds before hitting ground targets of importance, and later a naval variant also will be developed that can breach aircraft carrier groups and take out aircraft carriers in high oceans, but DRDO already has developed a hypersonic glide weapons system called Long Range Anti Ship Missile (LRAShM), but hypersonic cruise missiles will have much higher speeds and can operate at lower altitudes than glide weapons, making it much harder for enemy air defences to detect it until second before impact.
While the range of the missile will be over 1500 km, it has been said that even at Mach 8, a 1200-second burn will give the missile a range of over 2880 km, which will be nearly twice that of what was originally planned, but that doesn’t mean the missile will have such a range; the 1200-second test only proved that the engine’s thermal management can survive extreme heat without melting, and the actual real-world range might be anywhere between 1500 and 2000 km.
DRDO also has plans to develop a hypersonic attack cruise missile for the Indian Air Force to be launched from fighter jets.

articles.title: ICICI Prudential seeks $800m in latest credit push
articles.text: ICICI Prudential Asset Management Co. is seeking as much as $800 million for private credit and special opportunities funds, according to people familiar with the matter, tapping growing demand for alternative assets from wealthy investors and institutions.The Indian money manager aims to close its third private credit fund at about $500 million in December and is separately seeking up to $300 million for a special opportunities vehicle, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is private.Also read: Banks warn higher costs could hit demand as RBI weighs further repo hikeThe potential fundraising underscores the growth of private credit in Asia, which has largely avoided turmoil elsewhere as funds tend to be closed-ended and have limited software exposure. Indian managers have raised billions of dollars and are taking a growing share of the country’s lending deals from global firms, intensifying competition for managers such as Bain Capital and Davidson Kempner Capital Management.ICICI Prudential Corporate Credit Opportunities Fund has received commitments from more than a dozen insurance companies as well as family offices and wealthy individuals, said the people. The fund focuses on performing credit rather than distressed situations, typically providing capital to borrowers for expansion and other capital expenditure, they said.A spokesperson at ICICI Prudential AMC declined to comment. The firm is backed by ICICI Bank Ltd. and Prudential Plc. The UK-listed insurer owns about a third of the Indian money manager through Prudential Corp.Also read: AI is rewriting the rules of investment for India's big-ticket playersICICI Prudential AMC’s latest vehicle follows two private credit funds that raised about $160 million and $330 million, respectively, the people said. The manager has deployed money in companies including GMR Group, Puravankara Ltd. and Pinnacle Industries Ltd., the people said. The companies did not respond to emails seeking comment.

articles.title: Sensex surges 20% in dollar terms as foreign money chases India
articles.text: Mumbai: The Sensex has surged 20% in dollar terms this quarter, charging into what the Street describes as a bull-market zone, as record foreign fund flows in the fortnights either side of Diwali have made a sparkling rupee the envy of a dispirited Asia-Pacific in the throes of the AI meltdown."Around 15-16% of the gains in dollar terms came from rising share prices, while 4-5% was contributed by the rupee's appreciation," said Manishi Raychaudhuri, CEO of Hong Kong-based Emmer Capital Partners.Emerging market investors, who were significantly underweight on India, have been prominent buyers as funds move away from crowded AI trades toward the Indian markets, said Raychaudhuri.136086057The Sensex has logged the steepest gains since the Covid year after shrinking nearly a fifth in dollar terms through the first three quarters of 2026. The Nifty 50 has gained 18.2%, with both indices lately heading equity leader-boards globally.An index jump of 20% or more is widely regarded as the threshold for a bull market. This is more of a market convention rather than a formal rule.In rupee terms, both indices have risen around 16% each. The rupee has appreciated 3.4% against the dollar so far this quarter, boosting foreign investors' returns when their Indian investments are converted into the US currency.The last time the indices recorded sharper gains was in the December 2020 quarter, when both gauges rose nearly 26% in dollar terms.Read more: India does not have FANGs or MANGOes, but has WITCH companies, says PPFAS Mutual Fund’s Rajeev ThakkarSince October 16, when foreigners started buying stocks here again, overseas investors have pumped $14.33 billion, or approximately ₹1.43 lakh crore, into the market here. Of the 24 trading sessions since then, they have been buyers in 20."We've already seen some buying, but I think we're still at the 'beginning of the beginning', with scope for those inflows to continue over the coming months," said Ben Powell, chief investment strategist for the Middle East and Asia-Pacific, BlackRock Investment Institute.Powell said India's expanding workforce, rising productivity and digitalisation offered global investors diversification benefits at a time when many markets were becoming an "AI trade in disguise."Foreign investors had sold nearly $55 billion worth of Indian equities between October 2024 and September 2026. So far in the December quarter, FPIs invested $10.4 billion in India, the second-highest inflow after Japan's $48 billion.South Korea and Taiwan, investor favourites through early 2026, saw outflows of $26 billion and $57 billion, respectively, according to Bloomberg data.Read more: Nifty scales nine-month high, 26K in sight: 5 triggers that could drive or derail D-Street rally this weekThe rally comes as global markets have corrected amid concerns over AI and technology stocks, higher interest rates, inflation and policy uncertainty. During the same period, the S&P 500 fell 10%, while the Dow Jones and Nasdaq declined 5% and 16%, respectively. China's Shenzhen and Hang Seng indices lost 9% each, while Japan's Nikkei fell 16% in dollar terms. Taiwan's Taiex and South Korea's Kospi declined around 28%, Indonesia's Jakarta Composite fell 17%, and the Philippines lost 8%.The UK's FTSE 100 and Germany's DAX slipped 4% each, while France's CAC 40 declined 0.5%.Raychaudhuri said many investors were yet to return to the Indian market."There's still a significant population of investors who are on the sidelines of the India trade or who have just nibbled it a bit. The underweight positions on India were so large that it's difficult for it to have come to a neutral tilt in just about three weeks or so," he said.

$1 of GPT-5.1 tokens finds new ways around China’s Great Firewall
articles.text:
Researchers have found new ways to evade China’s Great Firewall after spending just $1 worth of tokens.

That result appeared last week in a paper titled “CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models” presented at the Conference on Computer and Communications Security run by the Association for Computing Machinery’s Special Interest Group on Security, Audit and Control.

Penned by six researchers from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Colorado Boulder, and activist group the Great Firewall Report, the paper points out that finding holes in the Great Firewall is a laborious process – so just the kind of task worth handing to AI.

The authors came up with a tool they call “CircumVolve” and describe as “a system for automated discovery of censorship circumvention strategies across the full network stack.”

“CircumVolve combines LLM code generation with iterative feedback-driven evaluation to produce verifiable and deployable evasion techniques,” they wrote. “CircumVolve models different censorship techniques as discrete scenarios, each capturing the specific context, protocol constraints, and blocking mechanisms of real-world censors. Within each scenario, evasion strategies are represented as executable Python programs that implement packet and protocol manipulations — from rewriting TCP/IP header fields, to crafting DNS queries that exploit parser ambiguities, to modifying the internal structure of encrypted QUIC Initial packets — while maintaining protocol correctness within tolerable bounds or strategically violating it when beneficial.”

The authors tested CircumVolve on simulated censorship tools used by China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, and on virtual private servers deployed on clouds in those countries. Those tests found the median API cost to the first successful evasion was less than $1 in token expenditure costs when using GPT-5.1.

The authors acknowledge that operators of censorship infrastructure might be able to observe CircumVolve at work, but feel its relatively small payloads – 80 KB of outgoing and 150 KB of incoming traffic – and 25-45-second pauses between tests might see it fly under the radar.

“CircumVolve represents a first step in leveraging LLMs to accelerate the censorship-circumvention lifecycle,” the authors wrote. “By automating the labor-intensive tasks of protocol analysis, implementation, and testing, AI-driven approaches make studying circumvention capabilities far more accessible to the comparatively under-resourced Internet freedom community [and] demonstrates how AI-assisted systems can narrow the resource gap between Internet freedom advocates and well-funded censoring states.”

Lenovo finally cracks monster datacenter profits

Ever since acquiring IBM’s x86 server business in 2014, Chinese hardware giant Lenovo has struggled to turn a profit from datacenter sales, even as it expanded its business into storage, networking, and selling to hyperscalers.

The AI boom has finally done what various strategy shifts and waves of hype could not: propel the company’s Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) to a $1 billion quarterly profit.

In its Q2 results announcement [PDF] last week, the company revealed ISG revenue hit a quarterly record of $11.3 billion, up 178 percent year-over-year, and that lovely big profit. At a time when enterprise hardware supply chains are tight, Lenovo says it was able to increase shipments of x86 servers and even emerge as the largest vendor of such systems with 16 percent market share.

Lenovo also claimed it’s moved further ahead as the planet’s premier PC provider, by pointing to 15 percent year-on-year growth for its intelligent devices group where quarterly revenue reached $17.4 billion. The company claims it has 23.8 percent of the PC market and now has seven percent more market share than its closest rival, Apple. The company said premium devices account for 63 percent of its PC business

Overall revenue rose 48 percent year over year to $30.24 billion for the quarter.

Indonesia’s glaciers are all but gone

It may surprise readers to know that Indonesia, the nation that spreads across 17,000 islands in the tropical latitudes of 11°S to 6°N, is home to alpine regions sufficiently high that glaciers can form.

Indonesia’s glaciers clung to the top of Puncak Jaya, aka Carstenz Pyramid, a 4,884-meter peak on New Guinea at 4°S.

Sadly, an assessment published last week by NASA says the glaciers have probably melted to the point at which not much is left other than a few patches of ice.

NASA last week posted images that show glaciers covering 4.31 km2 atop Puncak Jaya in 1988, and another from this year that shows most of that ice is gone. Images from September 2025 apparently showed just .09km2 of ice remained.

“To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts,” NASA’s Kathryn Hansen wrote. “Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.”

For what it’s worth, commercial operators run expeditions to Puncak Jaya. Peak-baggers seek it out because some consider it the highest mountain in Australasia/Oceania and therefore one of the “Seven Summits” – the highest point on each continent.

The Reg won’t get into the debate about the validity of including Puncak Jaya on that list, but if you fancy some equatorial alpine action your correspondent recently climbed Malaysia’s 4,095m Mount Kinabalu. It’s an overnight walk that requires no technical skills or gear, but definitely demands supple knees. The peak was clearly glaciated in the distant past but snow is now extremely rare on Kinabalu.

Australian bank giving away its bug-hunter

Here’s an odd one: Australia’s Commonwealth Bank (CBA) created an AI-powered tool to scan its bespoke code for bugs, and has now packaged it as a free release called “CodeCheck.”

The bank says analyzes the output of OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code with “a consistent process for analyzing code, investigating potential vulnerabilities and providing information to assist engineers.” Apparently, it is “ based on an approach used within CBA, but it is not the same as, and does not represent, the systems, tools or controls CBA uses internally.”

The bank posted CodeCheck to GitHub, where it warns the project is “a one-time open-source release for businesses to evaluate” and that it will not actively maintain, update, or support the code.

Japan’s space program hands some launches to Mitsubishi

Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) last week announced it has reached an agreement with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) to take over responsibility for running launches of its flagship H3 rocket when used in certain configurations.

The deal means MHI will handle launches for H3s that use a pair of LE-9 liquid-fuel engines alongside two SRB-3 solid-fuel boosters.

JAXA will continue running launches that use different, or experimental, configurations.

Once JAXA is satisfied those new rigs are reliable, it plans to transition them to private operators, too. ®
